newsitem.title: USA: U.S. shuttle crew test robot arm.
newsitem.headline: U.S. shuttle crew test robot arm.

text.p: The crew of the space shuttle Discovery on Friday tried out a prototype robot arm for the proposed international space station after releasing a satellite to gauge ozone depletion.
Astronauts Jan Davis and Steve Robinson flexed the five-foot (150 cm) mechanical arm mounted in the shuttle's cargo bay from a control panel in the cockpit.
The multi-jointed, dextrous arm, which cost the Japanese space agency about $100 million to develop, is designed to tend experiments mounted to the outside of a Japanese space station laboratory.

"It can open doors, undo bolts, replace things or maybe change out payloads that are sitting out on the back porch of the space station where we can't reach them," shuttle commander Curt Brown said on Friday.
Construction of the $60 billion space outpost was supposed to get underway this year, but was delayed until next June.

Discovery's crew achieved its primary objective less than eight hours after blasting off on Thursday, with the release of a German-built satellite that will gauge ozone depletion in the Earth's upper atmosphere.
Early on Friday, the astronauts could see the 7,000-pound (3,200-kg) spacecraft, known as CRISTA-SPAS, trailing Discovery by about 40 miles (65 km).
"CRISTA is awful beautiful in the sunrise," Brown told mission control. The spacecraft, which returned its first atmospheric measurements on Friday, will be retrieved by the shuttle on Aug. 16.
The shuttle pilots fired Discovery's manoeuvring jets to maintain formation with the free-flying satellite.
Other tasks planned during the 11-day mission included observations of Comet Hale-Bopp, monitoring of vegetation on Earth, and the growth of colon cancer cells for medical research.
Discovery is due to return to Earth at Florida'a Kennedy Space Centre on Aug. 18.
